items.item: A Region is a geographic grouping of multiple, independent data centers (AZs); an AZ outage and a Region outage are different, nested failure domains

at.step: One zone goes dark

items.item: Zonal vs regional is a property of the specific service, not of 'the cloud' generically — an operator has to check per service, not assume

at.step: Zonal vs regional vs multi-AZ by design, not by luck

items.item: A managed service's multi-AZ-ness is sometimes opt-in configuration (e.g. a database tier) rather than an automatic property of the service
Object storage is the canonical regional service: a single-zone request failure doesn't take the object's other replicas with it

at.step: Which of these three keeps serving?

items.item: Cross-AZ replication traffic is a distinct, named line item on a cloud bill, not bundled invisibly into compute or storage cost

at.step: What a zone outage actually costs to insure against

items.item: AZs within a region are close enough (within ~100km) for synchronous replication to be practical, which is why multi-AZ designs don't pay a cross-region latency penalty
A cell-based design is a deliberate trade: more operational surface (duplicated stacks, a routing layer, a rebalancer) bought for a smaller blast radius than the whole region

at.step: A cell is a smaller blast radius than a whole region

items.item: A cell boundary is meant to stop a software bug or bad deploy from reaching other cells' customers, not just a hardware/power failure

at.step: A cell is a smaller blast radius than a whole region

items.item: The practical habit this topic exists to build: before trusting a service with availability, check its specific, documented failure-domain guarantee rather than assuming 'the cloud handles it'

at.step: In one breath

items.item: Table formats and object-store-backed catalogs later in this course inherit their correctness from object storage's regional guarantee taught here — this topic is the floor the next one (object storage write/read semantics) stands on

A region, zone or cell boundary is a human-drawn abstraction over physical infrastructure (data centers, power grids, network paths) — it does not stop a sufficiently large, correlated physical event (a regional power grid failure, a submarine cable cut) from crossing it
